session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: I will frame participants as men in the UK who make food choices every day in specific social and personal contexts — not as people with views on nutrition policy or gender theory. The entry point will be the concrete and familiar: places, habits, routines. I want them speaking as themselves, from lived experience, before any more sensitive framing around gender or plant-based eating is introduced.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food identity: Participants may give socially polished answers ('gender doesn't really affect what I eat') that contradict specific behaviours they've already described — probe the behavioural level, not the abstract level, and watch for contradictions.

Social norms and peer influence: Participants may understate how much other men's reactions shape their choices — use concrete scenarios and past events to get below the surface of stated independence.

Plant-based shift: The imaginative leap in Section 4 ('what would need to change?') risks producing abstract wish-lists rather than specific friction points — ground immediately in their own described habits from Section 2.

Consensus risk around masculinity and meat: All five participants are meat-eaters; the group may quickly converge on a comfortable shared stance that meat is simply tastier or more satisfying, never surfacing the social and identity dimensions — plan early differentiation moves.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: At 20, the youngest in the group — may defer to older participants or may be more willing to challenge norms if he feels safe. Urban West Midlands context may bring a distinctive social eating culture worth drawing out.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Watch for deference to older voices; may need warm reactivation if he goes quiet in main topic sections.

known_risk_conditions: High social desirability risk on gender sections: men discussing gender and food in a group setting may gravitate toward liberal-presenting answers ('I just eat what I want, gender doesn't come into it') that mask real norm-governed behaviour — use behavioural anchors consistently.

Consensus around meat as default: all five are meat-eaters; rapid agreement that meat is simply better/more satisfying could foreclose exploration of identity and social dimensions — plan an early invite_dissent or sharpening probe if this emerges.

Plant-based questions may trigger mild defensiveness: participants may feel the session is nudging them toward a 'right answer' of eating less meat — take care to frame Section 4 and 5 as genuinely exploratory and not normatively loaded.

Will's rural context is distinct enough to create an implicit outlier dynamic — other participants may dismiss his perspective or he may self-censor to fit the urban majority; watch for this and create space for genuine contrast.
Amir as youngest may produce abbreviated or conformist answers under group influence — watch participation balance especially in the main topic sections.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–2 (intro and context): hold back significantly — allow self-introduction and early rapport to develop naturally, probe only if a genuinely rich cue appears. Section 3 (gender and food): shift to active moderation — this is where behavioural grounding, contradiction-surfacing, and consensus-breaking will matter most. Sections 4–5 (plant-based): push on specificity and friction points — resist abstract barriers and move participants toward concrete scenarios from their own lives. Section 6 (closing): light touch, open invitation, no new probing.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) carry the research weight and receive roughly 60% of the total budget. Context sections (1, 2) are warm-up and framing but still substantive — allocated moderately. Intro and closing are light; the intro scripted question is long but the responses will be short (name and location only).

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?

Amir has landed on: you can acknowledge structural shaping while remaining settled in your actual life — knowing something shaped you and being fine with it can coexist without full resolution.
Isaiah and Amir have converged on: you can acknowledge uncertainty about whether your preferences are shaped or genuine, and still just get on with your life without needing to resolve it.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was purely introductory — no substantive themes emerged yet. Participants established geographic identities (North East, Birmingham, Glasgow/Edinburgh, rural Scotland, Leeds), noted shared first-timer status, and built early rapport through mutual acknowledgment of uncertainty about the format. The dominant tone was cautious but warming, with mild regional solidarity beginning to surface (Ibrahim and Isaiah connecting as 'the northern lot'). The section closed with the moderator pivoting toward the first substantive question about social spaces.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator's approach here was deliberately light-touch: a warm, permission-giving opening designed to reduce performance anxiety and establish a conversational norm before any real content began. Framing it as relaxed and explicitly devaluing 'reasonable-sounding' answers was an attempt to pre-empt socially desirable responding. It appeared to work — participants responded naturally and briefly, without over-explaining themselves, and organic peer-to-peer acknowledgment emerged without prompting.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the relationship between place, infrastructure, and social connection — specifically how urban versus rural geography shapes the practicalities of male socialising. Conversation and comfort emerged as the genuine priority, with specific venues almost incidental to that. Weather and seasonality surfaced as a meaningful constraint, particularly for rural participants. The section stayed largely between two voices before broadening, with the dominant theme being adaptability to circumstance rather than preference for any particular setting.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section ran long on a two-person exchange between David and Will before I intervened to pull in the Birmingham, Newcastle, and Leeds voices. The intervention worked partially — Amir responded substantively and landed a useful reframe (conversation as the point, not the place) — but Ibrahim and Isaiah weren't heard before I moved to the next topic. I may have transitioned too quickly after Amir; holding briefly for the other two would have been worth the extra time.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the relationship between practicality and meaning in food decisions — participants initially framed their choices as purely functional (cost, convenience, habit), then collaboratively complicated that framing. The emergent theme was that unconscious, inherited eating patterns are both genuinely practical and socially shaped, without that undermining their legitimacy. Ibrahim introduced a secondary thread — defensive masculinity around meat-eating — which he himself named as embarrassing, opening a natural pivot toward gender.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: This section ran without moderator intervention until the transition — Isaiah and Ibrahim generated productive, self-correcting dialogue organically, so I held back deliberately. The risk was letting two voices dominate again, but the exchange had enough intellectual movement to justify it. The transition used Ibrahim's own language to bridge into the gender question, which felt earned rather than imposed. The remaining three participants still haven't been heard on food, which carries forward as a gap.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the tension between social conditioning and genuine choice — specifically whether shaped preferences remain authentic. A secondary thread examined the social visibility of dietary difference: vegetarianism 'marks' men out not through hostility but through requiring explanation, while meat-eating remains invisible as default. David's relative detachment from the masculinity-meat link introduced useful variation in how strongly this framing lands across participants, complicating any single account of male food identity.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section required pulling in the three quieter voices after Amir and Ibrahim ran a sustained two-person exchange. Framing the tension explicitly before redirecting worked — Will and David both added genuinely different perspectives rather than echoing. Direct address to David at the end was necessary given his sustained silence and paid off with the detachment contrast. The transition used Will's 'inside it' point as a concrete pivot toward practical acceptability, which felt earned. Coverage improved markedly compared to the previous section.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section deepened the earlier agency-versus-conditioning tension into a more granular question: can participants distinguish genuine preference from socialised default? Amir and David initially claimed confident self-knowledge — they'd choose meat anyway — before Ibrahim and Isaiah complicated this, arguing the neutral counterfactual is simply unavailable from inside a system that shaped you. Will added a rural-specific dimension: where alternatives aren't visible, even imagining a different choice is structurally foreclosed. Uncertainty emerged as the more honest position.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section opened with Amir and David running productively, so I held back until they'd resolved their exchange, then pulled in the three quieter voices with a single direct prompt. That worked — Isaiah and Ibrahim generated the most epistemically interesting content of the session organically, and direct address to Will surfaced a genuinely distinct rural angle. The transition used Will's availability point as a concrete pivot to the next question rather than a social-pressure reframe, which felt like the right seam.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section sharpened the earlier agency-versus-conditioning tension into a more personal and practical register: what would actually shift behaviour, and can 'not wanting' something be cleanly distinguished from never having had it normalized? A secondary theme emerged around liveable uncertainty — Amir and Isaiah both articulated a position where acknowledging that preference is shaped doesn't require resolving it or changing anything. Will's absence-versus-friction distinction added geographic texture beyond the rural infrastructure thread from earlier.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: I held back while David and Ibrahim ran a productive self-correcting exchange, intervening only when it risked becoming circular. Pulling in Amir, Will, and Isaiah sequentially worked — each added genuinely distinct positions rather than echoing. The callback to Amir's earlier gender remark was the most deliberate move: it surfaced a real tension he'd been sidestepping and got a more honest response. Isaiah's closing reflection landed well as a natural endpoint. Coverage across all five was strong this section.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This brief closing section distilled the session's central tension into its sharpest form: Ibrahim argued that not actively thinking about social pressure is categorically different from that pressure being absent. He pushed back on the 'liveable uncertainty' position reached earlier, insisting quiet, invisible conditioning still operates regardless of whether it's examined. The section didn't resolve the tension but gave it a harder, more uncomfortable edge than previous sections had.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: With only a closing contribution and sign-off here, there was nothing to manage beyond recognising a strong endpoint and not overwriting it. Letting Ibrahim's formulation stand without reframing or softening it was the right call — it crystallised a theme the group had circled all session, and imposed closure would have diluted that. The risk of ending on an unresolved tension felt preferable to false resolution.
